To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the majority of the patients with alcohol-related liver disease (ALDH) who underwent LT in our center did not relapse to heavy alcohol use and that the relapse rates were comparable to those of other studies.

the use of an addiction specialist team (AST) in the follow-up of patients with ALD who underwent LT was associated with a lower alcohol relapse rate and a lower rate of alcohol-related readmissions to hospital compared with patients who did not receive such a team.

1) the number of patients that were referred to the addiction team was higher in the second half of the observation period; 2) the number of consultations per patient was also higher in this period; 3) the number of alcohol-related complications was higher in the first half of the observation, and; 4) patients that were referred for a second time had higher rates of alcohol-related complications.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
alcohol use disorder (AUD) is a contraindication for liver transplantation.
the current data do not support a role for routine use of the MELD score for prioritization of liver transplantation for alcoholic hepatitis.
the use of a dedicated team of specialists in the field of addiction medicine in the context of LT for patients with ALD is of great importance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are able to provide a new method of treatment that is able to reduce the risk of relapse.

we have shown that there are no differences in the 1- and 2-year survival rates between the groups, but that there are differences in the 5-year survival rates, and that these differences can be explained by the differences in the incidence of relapse.

the most common reason for liver transplantation in the United States is alcohol-related liver disease, which accounted for 43% of all adult liver transplantations performed in 2015, followed by hepatitis C virus (HCV) at 26% (Schnitzler, 2016).
The main takeaway from our work is that
the role of the Addiction Specialist team in LT procedures is crucial for the success of the procedure.
the addiction team is a key component of the LT program and that its role should be clearly defined and its function well integrated within the transplant program.
the role of the addiction team in LT programs is to help the patients to stop drinking, stay abstinent and remain healthy for as long as possible after the transplantation.
